planting.note: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before last frost; sow successive plantings every 2-3 weeks for continuous harvest.

directions: Sow seed shallowly in cool, fertile soil and thin seedlings to 8-10 inches once they have several true leaves. Devil's Tongue is a small upright cos-type lettuce whose older outer leaves flush dramatically from light green to deep wine-red at the margins while new growth stays a contrasting fresh green, giving each head a striking mottled two-tone look. The heads stay relatively compact at 6-7 inches, so it works well in small beds or containers, and the crisp ribs and mild sweet flavor hold up better than many red lettuces as temperatures warm. Harvest whole heads once firm, or pick outer leaves individually for a longer cut-and-come-again harvest window.

planting.note: Start indoors 3-4 weeks before transplanting out around last frost; transplanting gives more uniform heading than direct seeding.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant out once seedlings have several true leaves, spacing 8-10 inches apart in fertile, moisture-retentive soil. Skyphos is a European-bred red butterhead prized for forming reliably dense, well-rounded heads even in variable weather, unlike many red butterheads that head loosely or split. Its deep burgundy-red outer leaves wrap around a contrasting lime-green heart, with color intensifying in cool weather and softening to more green in heat, and the buttery texture holds a mild, sweet flavor. It is a good choice for gardeners who want the visual drama of a red lettuce without sacrificing the reliable heading habit of a classic Boston type.

planting.note: Sow in late summer to fall for winter harvest under row cover or in a cold frame; also suitable for early spring sowing.

directions: Sow in late summer for a fall crop, or in early spring for a quick spring harvest; North Pole thrives in cold, short-day conditions and largely stops growing once winter cold sets in, then resumes as days lengthen. Small, unprotected plants can survive temperatures well below freezing, and with the light protection of a cold frame or row cover it reliably carries a crop of compact, buttery, lime-green heads through winter in cold climates. It resents summer heat and bolts quickly if grown in warm conditions, so it is best reserved for the coldest part of the lettuce calendar. Harvest whole heads once they feel dense, or pick individual leaves through the winter for a slower, extended harvest.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before last frost; fast-cropping habit suits tight succession planting schedules.

directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil and thin to 8-10 inches; Pomegranate Crunch is a medium-size red romaine bred for a texture between crisp romaine and tender butterhead, with thick, glossy cherry-red outer leaves wrapped around a heart that often blushes pink toward the center. It grows faster and more uniformly than many older red romaines while showing good resistance to downy mildew, making it a dependable choice for gardeners who want striking color without giving up productivity. The balance of sweetness and a light bitter edge suits both whole-leaf salads and Caesar-style preparations. Harvest as a full head once dense, or take outer leaves individually for an extended harvest.

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost; sow every 2 weeks for a continuous supply, and again in late summer for a fall crop.

directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed thinly in fertile, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist to slow bolting; Esmee is a fast, cold-tolerant arugula with deeply lobed, rounded oakleaf-shaped foliage that is fluffier and more ruffled than standard salad arugula, giving noticeably more visual loft in a mixed salad bowl. Its flavor leans nutty and mild rather than sharply peppery, making it approachable for gardeners and eaters who find standard rocket too pungent. Harvest baby leaves as early as three weeks for salad mixes, or let plants grow on for a fuller-size cutting at about six weeks. Like all arugula it bolts quickly in heat, so it performs best as an early spring or fall crop.

planting.note: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring harvest, and again in late summer for a fall and winter crop; resow every 7-10 days for continuous baby-leaf harvest.

directions: Direct sow into cool, fertile soil and keep consistently moist; Auroch produces large, oval, smooth, dark green leaves on an upright plant with long, sturdy stems, a habit that resists leaf damage and soil-splash from heavy rain better than more sprawling spinach types. It can be picked at any stage from baby leaf through full bunching size, giving flexibility for both quick salad greens and larger cooking leaves, and it shows strong resistance to multiple downy mildew races. It performs best as a fall, winter, or early spring crop and tolerates moderate winter cold with light protection. Cut whole plants at the base or harvest outer leaves individually to extend the picking window.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; excellent cold-soil germination suits very early sowing.

directions: Direct sow thinly into cool, moist, fertile soil as early as the ground can be worked, since Regiment germinates and establishes unusually well in cold soil. It produces dark green, semi-savoyed, arrowhead-shaped leaves on a fast-bunching plant that reaches harvest size in as little as five to six weeks, one of the quickest turnarounds among savoy-type spinach. Strong resistance to multiple downy mildew races keeps quality high through humid spring weather, and the leaves stay tender even as plants size up, reducing the pressure to harvest at a small stage. Cut whole plants at the base for bunching or pick outer leaves for a longer cut-and-come-again harvest.

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date; sow again in mid to late summer for a fall and winter crop in mild climates.

directions: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin seedlings to 8-10 inches apart. Orange Fantasia stands out among chards for its vivid, saturated carrot-orange stalks, midribs, and veining, a deeper and more solidly orange tone than the paler gold seen in yellow-stemmed chards, set against dark, glossy, savoyed green leaves. It is slow to bolt and holds its color well when cooked, making it a favorite for both the ornamental vegetable garden and the kitchen. Harvest baby leaves at about a month for salads, or let plants mature for six to eight weeks and harvest outer stalks continually, since the plant regrows from the center through a long season.
